common_name: Winter Beauty Witch Hazel (Fragrant Golden Late-Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, choosing a spot near a path or window where the leafless winter branches can be admired up close on gray days.

directions: This large, wide-spreading selection is grown for its especially heavy crop of twisted, deep gold ribbon petals set off by a dark red calyx, opening on bare wood in the depths of winter and carrying a notably strong, sweet fragrance that reaches well beyond the plant itself. Because it eventually forms a broad, multi-stemmed specimen rivaling many small trees, give it plenty of open ground rather than crowding it against a foundation. Keep the root zone evenly moist through summer, since flower bud set the following winter depends on the plant never drying out during the growing season. Little pruning is needed beyond removing crossing or damaged wood right after bloom finishes.

common_name: Sunburst Witch Hazel (Lemon-Yellow Fragrant Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in organically rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; its upright, ascending branch pattern keeps flowers held close to the stems rather than dangling loosely.

directions: Sunburst carries clean, clear lemon-yellow spidery flowers tight along the branches in late January and February, a slightly cooler tone than the more common golden or orange intermedia selections. Its upright, vase-shaped growth habit takes up less lateral room than spreading cultivars, making it a workable choice for a narrower side-yard planting. Bright green summer leaves shift to a good yellow-orange before dropping in fall, adding a second season of color. Water deeply during dry summer stretches and avoid heavy pruning, since flower buds form on the current year's wood well before winter bloom.

common_name: Gingerbread Witch Hazel (Burnt-Orange de Belder Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Install in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where the maroon-flushed new spring leaves and deep orange winter flowers can both be seen from a window.

directions: A de Belder nursery selection prized for its curled, strap-shaped flowers in a deep, smoky burnt-orange rarely seen elsewhere in the genus, set against a purple-red calyx for extra contrast on dull winter days. Emerging leaves are heavily washed in maroon-purple for several weeks each spring before greening up, giving the shrub a distinct look even outside the flowering period. Its moderately vigorous, spreading form is well suited to a mixed shrub border where it has room to widen without crowding neighbors. Mulch to hold consistent moisture and prune only lightly right after flowering, removing weak or dead wood.

common_name: Livia Witch Hazel (Long-Blooming Deep Red Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring in humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil that stays reliably moist in summer; four to six hours of direct sun daily brings out the deepest calyx and petal color.

directions: Livia opens deep red, lightly scented flowers with a matching purplish-red calyx over an unusually long window stretching from late autumn into late winter, and unlike many red-flowered witch hazels its petal color holds steady rather than fading as blooms age. Twiggy branching gives the shrub a somewhat denser, more spreading silhouette than the more upright intermedia cultivars, and spring foliage carries a heavy maroon-purple flush before turning medium green, with faint orange-red tones returning in fall. Keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season, since drought stress during summer directly reduces the following winter's flower show. Prune only to remove damaged or crossing wood immediately after flowering ends.

common_name: James Wells Witch Hazel (Golden Fragrant Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, giving it room to grow into a substantial multi-stemmed specimen over time.

directions: James Wells produces fragrant, golden-yellow, ribbon-petaled flowers set against a warm reddish-brown calyx, opening on bare branches during the coldest stretch of winter alongside the more widely planted intermedia selections. Its upright, gradually widening growth habit eventually forms a large, rounded winter-interest shrub suitable for the back of a mixed border or as a stand-alone specimen in a lawn. Consistent soil moisture through the growing season supports the following winter's bloom, while a dry summer often means a thinner flower display. Limit pruning to shaping cuts made right after flowering, since next winter's buds form soon afterward on new wood.

common_name: Rochester Witch Hazel (Copper-Orange Early Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; this selection tends to open its flowers earlier in the season than many other copper-toned intermedia cultivars.

directions: Selected at a public park in Rochester, New York, this cultivar bears strongly fragrant, straight, narrow copper-orange petals with red bases, opening earlier in the witch hazel season than many comparable orange-flowered selections. The shrub matures into a broad, rounded form of roughly equal height and spread, making it a good candidate for a specimen planting where its winter silhouette and bloom can both be appreciated from a distance. Give it steady summer moisture and a humus-rich, well-drained soil to keep the shallow root system from drying out. Prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead or crossing branches.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, strongly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, tucking it into a rock garden or small border where its unusually fine texture stands out against broader-leaved neighbors.

directions: Pygmaea is an oddity within the genus, its narrow, delicate, needle-like leaves giving the plant a fine, almost heath-like texture that barely resembles a typical broadleaf Pieris. Growth is extremely slow, and pendant clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers appear in spring without the bold new-growth color seen in most modern cultivars. Its diminutive, dense scale makes it a natural fit for a rock garden, trough, or the front edge of a small acid-soil border rather than a standard foundation planting. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic, and shelter from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, mulching to hold consistent moisture around the shallow, fibrous roots.

directions: Snowdrift is valued for its unusually long flower panicles, carrying an especially heavy load of pure white, bell-shaped blooms in early spring that noticeably outsize the trusses of the straight species. Coppery-bronze new growth in spring matures to a glossy, dense dark green, and the plant holds a tidy, mounding habit that resists the legginess some older Pieris cultivars develop with age. Its somewhat better cold tolerance than many japonica selections extends its usable range into colder gardens. Water during dry spells and prune only lightly right after flowering, since flower buds for the next season set soon afterward.

common_name: Red Mill Pieris (Fiery Red New-Growth Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; the brightest new-growth color develops when the plant is sheltered from intense midday sun.

directions: Red Mill produces some of the most vividly colored spring growth in the genus, with young leaves emerging a saturated fire-red before shifting through mahogany tones on their way to the mature glossy dark green typical of the species. Clusters of white, urn-shaped flowers open in spring beneath the new foliage, adding a second point of seasonal interest once the flush of color fades. Its medium-sized, well-branched habit works well as a specimen or as part of a mixed shade border alongside rhododendrons and azaleas. Keep the soil evenly moist and acidic, and prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain a full, dense form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade, siting it where the yellow-edged foliage can be seen up close since it is the plant's main year-round draw.

directions: Sold under the trade name Passion Frost, this patented selection pairs dark green foliage with a crisp buttery-yellow margin, and is notable for combining that variegation with unusually deep, antique-red bell-shaped flowers rather than the white blooms typical of variegated Pieris. Chains of flowers hang beneath the branches in early spring, giving way to a foliage display that carries interest through the rest of the year. Its compact, rounded habit suits a foundation planting, container, or the front of a shaded mixed border where the colorful leaf margin can be appreciated at close range. Grow in consistently moist, strongly acidic soil and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly to preserve the variegation.
